source.title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
source.authors: Leo Gao; Achyuta Rajaram; Jacob Coxon; Soham V. Govande; Bowen Baker; Daniel P. Mossing

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; some figures are represented as captions or flattened visual content.
record.tranche_reason: The paper investigates whether sparse training makes model components more interpretable and reports both reduced polysemanticity in some settings and residual polysemanticity, refining the scope of the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper does not quantify the share of polysemantic neurons. Its circuit-size and capability results use compact task-specific circuits as an interpretability proxy, not a direct polysemantic-neuron measure, so they are not recorded as claim-version rows. The text does explicitly report qualitative results about polysemantic features and monosemantic nodes.
record.test_reason: The study uses a different method, weight-sparse training, to ask whether a training choice reduces polysemantic nodes in transformer LMs. Its direct polysemanticity evidence is qualitative: sparse-model circuits still smear concepts across multi-task nodes, but much less than dense models (Sec. 5). Its main quantitative results use circuit size, a proxy, not a polysemantic-neuron rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that weight-sparse training yields much smaller, human-understandable task circuits whose nodes often match natural concepts. Sparsity trades capability for interpretability, and scaling total parameters improves the frontier. Scaling beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters remains hard, and bridges show preliminary promise for explaining dense models. They acknowledge that nodes are not fully monosemantic, though polysemantic smearing is much less than in dense models.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains weight-sparse transformers and prunes task-specific node circuits; it does not use the original vision-neuron feature-visualization procedure or the SoLU method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that activation sparsity has a non-monotonic relationship with the capability-interpretability frontier: increasing it initially helps, but further increases can make the frontier worse (Figure 37).

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-sparse models yield roughly 16-fold smaller task circuits than loss-matched dense models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sparsity makes task-specific circuits more compact, a circuit-size proxy rather than neuron polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing activation sparsity first improves, then worsens, the circuit-size vs loss frontier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation sparsity has a non-monotonic effect on the capability-interpretability frontier.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight sparsity raises residual-stream kurtosis (Fig. 10). Binarizability improves with total parameters (Fig. 34).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sparsity induces activation sparsity and more discretizable features.

record.problems: The paper does not estimate the proportion of polysemantic neurons. Its relevant polysemanticity findings are qualitative, and the pretraining-distribution example is explicitly cherry-picked. The paper also notes that its circuits are not fully faithful by causal-scrubbing standards.
record.rows_left_out: Circuit-size comparisons, capability-interpretability frontiers, and feature-binarization results were not included because they use proxies or measures other than polysemantic-neuron prevalence. These appear in Sections 3.1, 5, and Appendix C (Figures 2, 3, 34, and 37).

untested.parts: No prevalence or layerwise share of polysemantic MLP neurons in dense LMs is measured.
Superposition is cited as a hypothesized cause, but no test of feature count versus neuron count is made.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes when capacity is sufficient.
No quantified share of polysemantic neurons. No comparison with SoLU or convnets. The activation-function effect is not measured on polysemanticity directly.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No analysis of how activation-range choices or explanation scoring change polysemanticity labels.

missing.what: Capability/compute cost of the interpretability gain: sparser weights raise pretraining loss at fixed size, and sparse models need 100–1000x more compute.
Anecdotal architecture effect: small d_head (16) is said to improve monosemanticity of attention heads.
Randomly selected (non-dead) residual nodes are 'somewhat interpretable'; no dense comparison is given.
A methodological choice, forcing j=4 weights alive per neuron, may reduce the apparent monosemanticity of random nodes.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T2: the study does not argue V5 is wrong; it applies a different method to reduce polysemanticity. All direct polysemanticity evidence is qualitative. The quantitative results concern circuit size, a proxy. V5 verdicts therefore rest on authors' statements, not measured rates.

versions.untested_parts: The prevalence of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts in language models, including layerwise comparisons.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons, and whether features are packed together for capacity reasons.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is enough capacity for each feature.
The paper does not quantify the share of polysemantic neurons or compare SoLU and modern convolutional networks.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons in dense models detect a shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
How the measured prevalence of polysemanticity changes with activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

tranche.reason: A different method (weight-sparse training plus circuit pruning) aimed at disentangling superposition and polysemantic nodes, the question V5 asks. It does not argue that a version is wrong, so T5 is not needed.

source_check.notes: The polysemanticity evidence is one qualitative sentence in Limitations, with no counts or dense numbers. The study's quantitative interpretability metric (Figs. 2, 3, 37) is pruned circuit size, not polysemantic share. Sparse circuits are about 16x smaller than in a loss-matched dense model.

statements.problem: For this study: matches. GPT-2-style (Sec. 2.1), pretrained on Python code, and concepts smeared across nodes that also do other tasks 'to a much lesser extent than dense models'. Qualitative, no counts. Preprint with code; no CIs. Other studies' numbers not checked here.

Matches the text: residual smearing, especially in complex-task circuits (Sec. 5). At fixed total params, sparser weights harm capability but improve interpretability (Fig. 3). 100-1000x more compute than dense models of comparable capability (Sec. 5). Note that Fig. 3's interpretability is pruned circuit size, not a polysemanticity count.

This study's side is right: GPT-2-style LM trained de novo with weight sparsity on Python code. The evidence is a qualitative claim of much less smearing than dense models. Other study's details not checked here.

Fig. 37: increasing activation sparsity 'initially helps but eventually becomes Pareto dominated'. App. A.1 says too much activation sparsity hurts the frontier again. 'Non-monotonic' is a fair summary. The frontier's interpretability axis is circuit size. r1 holds the authors' polysemanticity reading of Fig. 37, not the non-monotonic pattern.
The only mention of this study is as reporting costs. That is correct: there is a capability trade-off at fixed total params (Fig. 3), and 100-1000x compute (Sec. 5).
